it1.intro: The Giuoco Pianissimo. Both bishops come to the active diagonals, and White keeps the centre closed with c3 and d3.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
Bc5 develops the dark-squared bishop and aims at the pawn on f2. Black copies the idea.
c3 prepares a central pawn and takes b4 away from the dark-squared bishop. White is staying quiet.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
d3 supports the pawn on e4 and frees the dark-squared bishop. The centre stays closed.
d6 supports the pawn on e5 and frees the light-squared bishop. Black matches the quiet centre.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
a6 takes b5 away from White's pieces and gives the dark-squared bishop a square to drop to.
a4 gains a little queenside space and stops Black pushing a pawn there.
Ba7 steps the dark-squared bishop back along its diagonal, still looking toward the pawn on f2.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight without blocking the c-pawn. It can support the centre or reroute.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Both kings are safe, and the centre is still closed.
h3 stops a piece landing on g4 and gives the king a little air. The knight on f3 is left in peace.
Ne7 reroutes the queen's knight toward the kingside. g6 is the square it wants.
Re1 puts the rook on the e-file behind the pawn on e4, ready for a central break.
Ng6 brings the knight to the kingside. Black's pieces lean that way while the centre stays closed.

it2.intro: The main Two Knights. After the knight jumps toward f7, d5 and Na5 are the sound answer. This is not the Fried Liver.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4. This is the Two Knights.
Ng5 attacks the pawn on f7. Black should answer in the centre, not by grabbing.
d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and the knight's idea. A central pawn is the right reply.
exd5 takes the pawn on d5. White accepts the pawn, and Black will chase the bishop.
Na5 attacks the bishop on c4. Chasing the bishop is the sound move in this line.
Bb5+ gives check and steps the light-squared bishop off the knight. The check wins a moment.
c6 attacks the bishop on b5 and attacks the pawn on d5. Black wants the pawn back and the bishop off.
dxc6 takes the pawn on c6 and opens the queenside.
bxc6 recaptures the pawn on c6. The b-file is half-open, and the pawn on e5 remains Black's centre.
Be2 drops the light-squared bishop back to a safe square. It has done the checking job.
h6 asks the knight on g5 a question. The knight should not be left sitting there.
Nf3 drops the knight back into play. The jump toward f7 is over.
e4 pushes the pawn and gains space. The pawn on e4 cramps White's centre.
Ne5 plants the knight on a central square and attacks the pawn on c6.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks the knight on e5. Black is ready to castle.

it3.intro: The Hungarian. Black plays the modest bishop to e7, White opens with d4, and the game stays controlled.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
Be7 is the Hungarian. The dark-squared bishop stays modest and leaves the centre for White to open.
d4 opens the centre at once. Against this passive bishop, White does not stay quiet.
exd4 takes the pawn on d4 and accepts the open game.
Nxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and puts a knight in the centre.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Black gets the king out before the centre grows.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
d6 supports the centre and frees the light-squared bishop. Black keeps a compact shell.
h3 gives the king air and stops a piece landing on g4.
Nxd4 takes the knight on d4. Black removes the central knight.
Qxd4 recaptures the knight on d4. The queen takes the centre.
c6 keeps White's pieces off b5 and d5 and prepares ...d5 against the bishop on c4.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop to an active square. White's pieces are comfortably placed.
Be6 offers a trade of the light-squared bishop that sits on c4. Black finishes the development of the minor pieces.

it4.intro: A solid d6. The queen comes to b3, and taking the knight on h6 drags the g-pawn away from the king.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
d6 supports the pawn on e5 and keeps the dark-squared bishop inside for a move. This is a solid, slightly cramped choice.
c3 prepares a central pawn and takes b4 away from Black's pieces.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling. The light-squared bishop is still at home.
Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7 and stands behind the bishop on c4. The pressure is toward f7.
Nh6 develops the king's knight to an awkward square so the pawn on f7 stays defended. The knight can be taken.
d4 opens the centre. The queen is already on b3, so White is ready for open lines.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The knight on h6 is the piece White wants.
Bxh6 takes the knight on h6. Black's g-pawn is the recapture, and that opens the king's side.
gxh6 recaptures the bishop on h6. The pawn in front of the king has been dragged off its square.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. White castles into a healthier kingside.
Bg5 steps the dark-squared bishop out to an active square.
Na3 develops the queen's knight toward the centre. b5 and c4 are squares it can use.
Kh8 tucks the king into the corner, off the half-open file the g-pawn left.
Rfe1 puts a rook on the e-file. The pawn on e5 is the target if the centre opens.
a5 gains queenside space and slows the knight on a3. Black looks for counterplay away from the king.

it5.intro: A fianchetto against the Italian. White's knight visits g5, then both sides finish development and Black castles.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
g6 prepares a fianchetto. The dark-squared bishop will use the long diagonal.
d3 supports the pawn on e4 and frees the dark-squared bishop. White stays flexible against the fianchetto.
Bg7 puts the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal. It eyes the centre from g7.
Ng5 attacks the pawn on f7 and probes the kingside. The knight is a nuisance, not a sacrifice.
Nh6 defends the pawn on f7 and develops the king's knight. The square is awkward, which is the point of the probe.
a4 gains queenside space before the knight drops back.
f6 kicks the knight on g5. The pawn also takes the natural square from the king's knight, which is why it went to h6.
Nf3 drops the knight back to its proper square. The probe is over.
Nf7 improves the knight from h6. It can support the centre and cover the kingside.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and eyes the centre.
d6 supports the pawn on e5 and frees the light-squared bishop.
Be3 develops the dark-squared bishop and opposes the bishop on g7.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king sits behind the fianchetto, and White still has to castle.

it6.intro: A quiet Two Knights with d3. Black castles, then the knight from a5 takes White's light-squared bishop on b3 and the a-file opens.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4. This is the Two Knights, met quietly.
d3 supports the pawn on e4 and frees the dark-squared bishop. White declines the sharp knight jump.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling. Black stays solid.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Both kings are safe before the queenside tension.
Re1 puts the rook behind the pawn on e4, ready to support the centre.
d6 supports the pawn on e5 and frees the light-squared bishop.
c3 prepares a central pawn and gives the light-squared bishop a square to drop back to.
Na5 attacks the bishop on c4. Black wants to trade the knight for that bishop.
Bb3 keeps the light-squared bishop and steps off the knight. White offers the trade on b3 rather than giving the bishop away for nothing.
Nxb3 takes the light-squared bishop on b3. That was the point of sending the knight to a5.
axb3 recaptures the knight on b3. The a-file is half-open for the rook.

it7.intro: The Greco trap in the classical Italian. Taking the pawn on c3 with the bishop walks into Ba3 and Bb5, with the king still in the centre.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
Bc5 develops the dark-squared bishop and aims at the pawn on f2. Black is playing the classical Italian.
c3 prepares the central break and takes b4 away from the bishop for a moment. The centre is about to open.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
d4 opens the centre. This is the classical Italian, not the quiet pawn line.
exd4 takes the pawn on d4 and accepts the open game.
cxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and builds a classical pawn centre.
Bb4+ gives check. The dark-squared bishop uses the check to reach an active diagonal, and White blocks with the knight.
Nc3 blocks the check and develops the queen's knight. The bishop on b4 pins that knight to the king.
Nxe4 takes the pawn on e4. The knight in the centre starts the greedy sequence.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king leaves before the tactics, and the rook will like the open file.
Nxc3 takes the knight on c3. Black is grabbing, which is what the trap wants.
bxc3 recaptures the knight on c3. The b-file is half-open, and the pawn is bait.
Bxc3 takes the pawn on c3. That greedy capture is the mistake.
Ba3 develops the dark-squared bishop onto the diagonal toward f8. Black cannot castle while this bishop eyes that square.
d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and tries to get air. The king is still on e8.
Bb5 pins the knight on c6 to the king on e8. The king stays in the centre.

it8.intro: Two Knights with b5. The bishop drops back to f1, the queen takes the pawn, and White takes on b5 once the queen has moved.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4. This is the Two Knights.
Ng5 attacks the pawn on f7. Black should answer in the centre.
d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and meets the knight on g5 in the centre.
exd5 takes the pawn on d5. The pawn on d5 is now the target.
b5 attacks the bishop on c4 and gains space. Black does not take the pawn back with a piece yet.
Bf1 drops the light-squared bishop home, off the pawn on b5. The bishop will come back out once the queen has moved.
Qxd5 takes the pawn on d5 and develops the queen into the centre. She will be asked to move.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the queen on d5.
Qc5 steps the queen off the knight and keeps her active. The knight on c3 now covers b5, so the pawn there can be taken.
Bxb5 takes the pawn on b5. The knight on c3 defends the bishop, so it is safe there.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
d3 supports the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Black is castled, and White still needs to castle.

it9.intro: The Centre Attack. White pushes e5 instead of taking on d4, and the dark-squared bishop ends on b6.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
Bc5 develops the dark-squared bishop and aims at the pawn on f2.
c3 prepares the central pawn push.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
d4 attacks the bishop on c5 and opens the centre. This is the Centre Attack.
exd4 takes the pawn on d4. Black accepts the opening of the centre.
e5 kicks the knight on f6 and does not take the pawn back yet. White wants the knight off before recapturing.
d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and claims the centre. Black strikes back instead of retreating the knight.
Bb5 pins the knight on c6, because the d-pawn has left its home, and steps the bishop off the pawn on d5.
Ne4 steps the knight off the pawn on e5 and into the centre.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and restores a pawn in the centre. The file opens.
Bb6 keeps the dark-squared bishop and steps off the pawn on d4. The bishop still looks down its diagonal.

it10.intro: Two Knights with an early d4. The centre pushes on, White's light-squared bishop takes on c6, and White castles.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The Italian puts that bishop on the diagonal toward f7.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. This is an open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 is the Italian. The light-squared bishop aims at the pawn on f7, the soft point in front of the king.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4. This is the Two Knights, and White opens at once.
d4 opens the centre immediately. White does not play the quiet pawn or the knight jump.
exd4 takes the pawn on d4 and accepts the open centre.
e5 kicks the knight on f6. White pushes past the pawn on d4 instead of taking it.
d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and claims the centre.
Bb5 steps the light-squared bishop off the pawn on d5 and attacks the knight on c6.
Ne4 steps the knight off the pawn on e5 and into the centre. This knight is Black's active piece.
Nxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and puts a knight in the centre. The earlier pawn push has done its job.
Bd7 develops the light-squared bishop and breaks any pin on the knight on c6.
Bxc6 takes the knight on c6. White is happy to trade the light-squared bishop for that knight.
bxc6 recaptures the bishop on c6. The c-pawns are doubled, and the b-file is half-open.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king is safe, and the knight on e4 is the piece to watch.
